The last switchboard operators are retiring
A job that once employed thousands now has fewer than forty people left in it, and the last of them are going.
July 17, 2026

Fewer than forty switchboard operators remain in federal service. (iStock)

Her father worked the same board for thirty-one years, and when she took the job in 1994 he gave her a pair of cotton gloves and told her the trick was to keep her wrists loose and her voice lower than she thought it needed to be.

It was not easy, but she was hooked.

Most of the remaining boards sit in buildings that have been scheduled for demolition twice, and the operators have learned to treat each reprieve as a year rather than a promise, which is how you get thirty-one of them.

Nadia Okonkwo at the board she has worked since 1994. (Courtesy of the Okonkwo family)

The switchboards were never meant to outlast the buildings around them, and yet a handful of them have, humming in basements under offices that emptied out years ago and were never filled again.

A retired board sits in storage outside Baltimore. (Marta Lindqvist/AP)
